Mr. Speaker, the answer is as follows:
1.	The income tax assessments issued to John C. Doyle for the years 1950, 1953 and 1954 are presently under appeal to the tax appeal board and the amount of tax payable has not been finally determined. In order to secure payment of the ultimate tax liability, the Department of National Revenue filed a certificate of tax liability and took out a writ of extent in the Exchequer Court of Canada on July 8, 1963 for the income tax assessed for those years. Shares of Jubilee Iron and of other companies were seized under this writ.
2.	From the date of the writ of extent, 220,000 shares of Jubilee Iron were taken into the custody of the Exchequer Court. The Exchequer Court order of December, 1965, permitted Mr. Doyle to convert the shares into cash at not less than $3 per share, the proceeds to be retained in the custody of the court pending determination of the amount of the tax liability. 3.	None of the seized shares of Jubilee Iron Corporation have been sold. Their present quoted market value is around $2 per share.

It has come to be recognized that the Department of Veterans Affairs has pioneered several fields in the administration of pensions and social legislation. A great deal of the work which has been done by the Canadian Pension Commission over the years has been studies by workmen's compensation boards across the country, and in some cases their methods have been patterned on the experience and practices of the commission. I think it is right to give credit where it is due, though on some occasions of course we differ from the views of the commission.
The Veterans Land Act was a pioneer measure in the field of supervised credit. For a number of years this work was undertaken by the department, and the results were watched. It is because of the experience of the administration of the Veterans Land Act with respect to the supervision of farm credit that the Farm Credit Act was brought into being.
The department has also pioneered research into the development of artificial limbs, not only to the advantage of veterans but now, because of recent arrangements, to the advantage of all Canadians who require this service.

From April 17 to April 22, the 21st convention of the Royal Canadian Legion was held in Montreal. I, together with some other members of the committee, attended as members of the standing committee on veterans affairs. We were very interested in the organization of this convention and in its conduct. Let me say without any hesitation that it was a demonstration of democracy in action. There was no question, there, of delegates lining up at microphones and being cut off without having an opportunity to speak. I heard of another convention where delegates lined up at three different microphones, but they were cut off and the question decided by a show of hands without all the delegates wishing to speak being heard.
At this convention, any delegate coming from any part of Canada, whether five miles from Montreal or 3,000 miles away, was given an opportunity to present his views on any resolution which came before the assembly. This is what was done, and I think it was a demonstration of the functioning of democracy which might well be copied by some other organizations in Canada.
No guillotine there.

No guillotine whatever. And, on occasions, when you get some of these older veterans before a microphone they take a little time to express their views. They can be a little trying on occasions. I am sure I am trying to some of my colleagues on occasion.
Oh, frequently.

I am glad to know it. It shows I am effective.
But these men were listened to-sometimes apparently, with little sympathy from the delegates around them. But the chairman said: Everybody is going to be heard. And apparently everybody was heard, before the question was put on any resolution.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Now, Mr. Chairman, resolutions arising from that convention will in due course be presented by the Royal Canadian Legion to the standing committee on veterans affairs.
June 15, 1966

Supply-Veterans Affairs There were resolutions with respect to amendments to the Pension Act, the Veterans Land Act, the education assistance act, the administration of D.V.A. hospitals, the armed forces and civil defence, the latter being a very constructive one, and also proposals with respect to a history of Canada for our centennial year. All members of the committee present at the convention were impressed by the serious approach taken to these matters by the representatives of veterans and their dependants, who total approximately 4 million people.
With those few remarks I shall conclude, and trust that later on this year we will have an opportunity to hear representations from the organizations I have mentioned, and others, so that we will be able to make a report to the house that the government will feel inclined to accept.

Mr. Chairman, the Social Credit party was not able to have a member on the veterans affairs committee this session. Therefore I wish to make a few remarks on this occasion and indicate our support for some of the statements made this afternoon, and to present several proposals that we feel should be emphasized.
I want to join with those who have expressed confidence in the Minister of Veterans Affairs and his officials, and in their sincere efforts to eliminate some of the inequities that still remain in veterans legislation. I have heard many veterans say that this Canadian legislation is among the best in the world. They appreciate that fact; yet there are several problems that still need to be resolved. This is not in any way to question the sincerity of the minister or his officials, or of those who served in like capacities in days gone by. It is just a recognition of the fact that problems arise and that new information comes to hand which points out the need for additional remedial action.
I first wish to mention the question of disability pensions. There has been considerable discussion in the house on this problem. It was raided on many occasions in past years when 1 had the opportunity to serve on the veterans affairs committee, but to date the government has not been able to come up with a satisfactory solution. I appreciate the reference that has been made to the commission that is presently studying this matter, and I hope in the near future action will be taken on it.
[Mr. Herridge.i
Due to the increased cost of living and other factors which enter into the matter, all hon. members are aware of the need to pay constant attention to the requirements of pensioners in all categories. I would draw attention to a resolution on this subject which appears at page 24 of the June edition of The Legionary, and which reads as follows:
Therefore be it resolved that the Royal Canadian Legion renew its request for an immediate increase in the basic rate of disability pension to bring this in line with the salaries of civil servants, which can only be done by increasing the basic rate without further delay to $3,880 per annum.
We in this group heartily support that resolution and ask that attention be given toward providing an immediate increase in the disability pension. Just yesterday I received a letter from a veteran in my own constituency calling this problem to my attention once again.
Another matter which has been brought to my attention by veterans and their organizations in my area has to do with war veterans allowance recipients and their eligibility for old age security benefits. At page 26 of the same issue of The Legionary there appears this resolution:
Therefore be it resolved that old age security be considered as exempt income under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
There is a lengthy preamble to the resolution, setting out the basic reasons why the Legion feels justified in making this request. Once again we in this party give it our support and ask that it be given favourable consideration.
Another matter which I have mentioned in this house from time to time is the application of the benefit of doubt clause. The feeling exists in the minds of many veterans that this clause actually works in reverse, and instead of the commission placing the interests of a veteran first and foremost, many people feel the clause is being used to try to get out of meeting the needs of various veterans. I trust this will be taken into consideration by the department.
I am glad to note the special attention that has been given to the Hong Kong veterans during the course of the veterans affairs committee proceedings. These are in a class by themselves, with particular needs and particular problems, having suffered conditions that were worse than those which many other veterans were called upon to endure.
June 15, 1966	COMMONS
I know the committee has recommended the adoption of the report and passage of the estimates. We agree with this procedure, but we are glad to have this opportunity to bring these matters to the attention of the minister at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to join in general with the observations that have already been made, which in every way have been characterized by that freedom from political considerations that has always been a rule in the house when dealing with veterans affairs.
When the hon. member for Kootenay West made reference to the convention of the Royal Canadian Legion it came to my mind that it was during the lifetime of the administration of which I had the honour to be the head that I was able to recommend to Her Majesty the addition of "Royal" to the name of the Canadian Legion. That was accepted by Her Majesty, and this was the first time among the Legion organizations that this high and honourable designation had been permitted and allowed.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
When I look back over the years, from time to time I am reminded that it was 50 years ago that I had the honour of joining His Majesty's forces. Throughout the period, since the time of the foundation of the Canadian Legion, I have been an active member, until, as is the case with all who have been prime minister of this country, that great body of Canadians conferred upon me the honour of a life membership.
Today, instead of dealing in general with many of the matters which have been considered so thoughtfully by the committee, I am going to restrict myself to just one thing. It is of course known that my views do not coincide with those of others in this house who have an inexorable urge to bring about the committees system. Throughout my period of office, and also while in opposition, my experience has been that the committees system does not operate effectively under parliamentary government. There are exceptions. Those exceptions have to do with matters which are not of a partisan nature and which therefore command the general support of members of the committee. There were those with stars in their eyes in this parliament, as in previous parliaments, who have strongly advocated the committees system.
DEBATES	6453
Supply-Veterans Affairs 1 am one of those who do not accept the committees system as being effective under parliamentary government. I think the experience of the last few months at least might be cited, for, on several occasions, committees have found it necessary to apply to the house for a reduction in their quorum, those reductions being of such a nature as to reduce the committees to virtual inoperation. According to reports, committee after committee has had to adjourn because of lack of a quorum. I should like to point out again that one major exception is the veterans affairs committee, which brings together the members of this house in that fraternity of comradeship which gives them a desire to contribute their best each year during the meetings of this committee.
During the days of the last war those who were ex-service men and ex-service women used to meet together from time to time at dinners and other social functions. I can tell you that those functions were clear evidence that members of this house, however divergent their opinions may be politically, lose all sense of condemnation of one another because of the fact that they have been partners in the service of their country.
The particular item to which I wish to refer has to do with the injustice, as I see it, that is suffered by the veterans who receive the war veterans allowance, better known as the "burnt out" pension. Those who served in the first world war, with the exception of members like the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre who served at the front line in both world wars and who seem to have found the elixir of everlasting youth, are showing their age. Today only a few are under 70 years of age, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre being one of the exceptions. Many of these veterans are in financial difficulties and straitened circumstances. It is only because they are in financial difficulties in so far as their income is concerned that they receive the war veterans allowance.
I believe Canadians as a whole would support action to remove what many of them believe to be an injustice, namely that, when they become entitled to the old age pension, their war veterans allowance is reduced, the pension being considered as income. Therefore they are denied full privileges in respect of payment under the War Veterans Allowance Act. These men feel a sense of deep injustice. If they had not served, they would receive the old age pension, old age security, or whatever you may designate it. It is theirs

June 15, 1966
Supply-Veterans Affairs by right; every person whatever his or her financial position is entitled to the payment oi the old age pension. They have a very logical argument. Why should they as men and women who served, and whose income otherwise is below the level for entitlement to the war veterans allowance, be discriminated against in the manner in which they now are?
The hon. member for Vegreville, as well as hon. members in all parts of the house, has mentioned this on more than one occasion. Surely this is one change which we could make. The argument is that if we do so, some time long in the future, when young men like the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who served with distinction in the second world war, will have attained the age of qualification for the old age pension, the charge against the public treasury will be a very considerable sum. When we were in office we were faced with this. When parliament passed the last increase in the old age pension, the $10 increase, we specifically provided that the amount of that increase should not be taken into consideration as income which would result in a reduction of the war veterans allowance.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
It has been said that it will cost the country something to take this stand and make it of general application, but let us not forget to count the cost to those who served and are entitled to war veterans allowances. This cost is something that still causes irritation and annoyance, and sometimes the expression of words that are not completely parliamentary.
The minister in his position, like his predecessors, has administered the department in a way that assures a high degree of responsibility and justice to those who served. While I do not often inject myself into these debates on estimates I am making an appeal to the minister to do something effective in this regard. Dr. Richardson went fully into the contemplated action that is to be taken with regard to Hong Kong veterans. There is no limit, as I see it, to the favourable reaction that would come from those old soldiers who, today, cast their longer shadows toward the east, and it would be a wonderful thing in our centennial year of confederation for Canadians as a whole to express their thoughts of appreciation to those who served by removing from them what they feel so often is an injustice and unfairness.

It is in that spirit that I give the strongest possible support to action being taken. These people are nearing the end of their road and they have given everything. We spend tens of millions of dollars on other things, yet those things would never have been in existence but for the services of those men and women who served. I know that the minister, all who have served, and, indeed all Canadians, would look with favour on action in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to make any extended remarks at this time because, as other speakers have pointed out, these estimates have been examined very thoroughly by the standing committee, which was unanimous in recommending that they be given speedy approval by this house.
I should, however, like to associate myself with the compliments that have been paid to the chairman of the committee on veterans affairs by those who have preceded me, for the manner in which he carried out his duties and for the fair and impartial way in which he presided over its deliberations. I have been a member of that committee now for 17 years and I do not think I have ever attended any meetings of a former committee at which the zeal of members to safeguard the welfare of veterans and give sympathetic consideration to their problems surpassed that of the members of the committee which has just rendered its report.
I want to express my appreciation also to the minister, the officials of his department, the heads of the agencies of that department including the Canadian Pension Commission, the war veterans allowance board, the Veterans Land Act Administration, the veterans bureau, and the chairman, vice chairman and directors of those agencies for the warm and sympathetic consideration they have always given to the problems of veterans. These people are uniquely fitted to deal with human problems and they are the members of at least one department to which people are more important than material things.
It is evident from representations made by various veterans organizations, members of the standing committee and members of this house that the present basis upon which veterans pensions are determined is no longer adequate, but still a modification of the original basis which was related to salaries or wages paid to unskilled labour. The spirit in which the veterans charter was presented to and passed in this house many years ago was
June 15. 1966

that the veteran was entitled to special treatment over and above the average citizen because of his service to this country, his willingness to serve and risk everything so that the rest of us might be free. That spirit has pervaded our approach to veterans legislation, and nowhere has this been more evident than at the meetings of the present parliamentary committee on veterans affairs.
The time has arrived when we must seek a new basis on which to calculate veterans pensions. I have given some thought to this matter and I should like to put forth the suggestion that we explore the possibility of using the median of civil service salaries as the basis. I have not had time to find out how that median of the last three or four years would compare with the present scale of pensions, but at least it would be a constant basis to be used year after year and would tie up with the cost of living increment calculated over several years.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Let me point out to the house that I am referring to the median and not the average civil service salary. The median salary is the salary where the number of salaries below is equal to the number of salaries above it. That is the possible basis upon which I suggest veterans pensions might be calculated.
Many other things could be discussed in relation to the Pension Act and the operation of the Pension Commission, but since there is a committee under Mr. Justice Wood examining these matters I think it would be wise to defer any further comment in this regard until he has presented his report.
There are several other matters which I should like once again to bring to the attention of the minister. When I was sitting on the other side of the house I advocated certain things, and I want to go on record now as being still as strongly in favour of them as I ever was in the past. The first of these matters is perhaps a local affair because it has to do with the Newfoundland foresters who served overseas in world war II. We have been advocating for many years that the foresters and seamen be brought under the veterans charter. I do not think this would cost very much in terms of dollars, because they would not receive very much monetary benefit beyond what they are now receiving under the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act, but I think it would be a recognition of their service which they have been
Supply-Veterans Affairs seeking so long to attain. While I am talking about the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act I should like to bring to the minister's attention the fact that there is a clause in it which discriminates between merchant seamen and foresters. A merchant seaman can qualify for a civilian war allowance provided he served for a period of six months and during that time made at least one trip in dangerous waters.
There are many foresters of world war II who served overseas for six months but are debarred from receiving the civilian war allowance because the act contains a clause which requires them to have signed on for the duration. The first contingent of foresters recruited in Newfoundland was signed up under a contract for six months. They had no option to sign any other contract at that time and no option afterwards, except to renew their contract for a further period. It thus happens that many who served overseas for four years are still debarred from receiving the allowance just because of the technicality that they did not sign up for the duration. When they see a merchant seaman living next door in their own village who served six months and qualified for this allowance they feel, and I think justly so, that they have been discriminated against. I would ask the minister to look into this matter and try to find some way of eliminating this "duration" clause from the legislation.
I should like also to support the representations made by my hon. friend from Vegreville on behalf of the removal of the 3 65-day clause in the War Veterans Allowance Act with respect to veterans of world war I. There are not very many veterans of world war I left. We learned in committee that their average age now is 72. I have been informed by the chairman of the War Veterans Allowance Board that if this clause was eliminated and every veteran who might possibly qualify automatically became eligible, the total cost would be somewhere around $7 million. Of this figure $4 million would be for the increase in allowance and the other $3 million would be for the cost of treatment services, because a recipient of war veterans allowance is automatically entitled to free treatment.
I should like to point out to the minister and the committee that this figure of $7 million is based on the assumption that every single veteran left would qualify. We know this would not be so because the War Veterans Allowance Act has a means test and I
June 15. 1966

Supply-Veterans Affairs doubt very much whether half of these people would qualify; I think half are well enough off that their financial circumstances would not permit them to qualify under the act in any case. This means that the total cost in one year would be somewhere around $3 million, perhaps $3J million, of which $2 million would be for the payment of the allowance and the other $1J million would be for treatment. Since they are 72 I think we can safely say that in 10 years time, by the time they reach the age of 82, the amount expended on these veterans would be negligible.
This means that the average total cost over 10 years would be only around $2 million a year. Time is running out for these old veterans, and in view of the rising cost of living many of them now need additional help. In view of the desire of the people of Canada to give the veteran a little special treatment above that afforded the ordinary citizen, to keep him from going on public relief, I think this 365-day requirement could very well be eliminated from the legislation. The cost to the treasury, when compared with our huge budgets covering expenditures of $7 billion, would be practically negligible.
The only other point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee also has to do with the War Veterans Allowance Act. This matter concerns the clause which requires a veteran under 60 to be totally and permanently unemployable before he can qualify for war veterans allowance. I think when the War Veterans Allowance Act was introduced we had in mind the old veterans of world war I. We have not paid much attention to the fact that there are now many veterans of world war II who are under 60 and because of their physical condition are no longer able to work. These veterans and their families are suffering real hardship and there is no way in which they can obtain relief because there is in the act this clause requiring that they be totally and permanently unemployable and incapable of maintaining themselves. With the advances that have been made by medical science in recent years it is almost impossible for anyone to be classified as totally and permanently unemployable. If a veteran is unable to work for a period of six months or a year this causes very real hardship and distress to himself and his family, and I believe he is entitled to expect some relief under the veterans charter.


Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would ask two things: First, that we modify this requirement of being totally and permanently unemployable and, second, that some other means be provided in the War Veterans Allowance Act to supplement the war veterans allowance. The old war veterans who qualify can have extra income up to $220 a month. In addition they can go out and earn $900 a year in casual work. But the young veteran, the veteran of world war II who is unemployable, who is practically an invalid, cannot do this. He cannot work; he cannot supplement his allowance by casual earnings-and very often he has more obligations than those of the world war I veteran because he probably still has children attending school.
He can get only the maximum allowance, which is $161 a month. I believe some method should be devised of supplementing the maximum allowance for the veterans of world war II. I would be very grateful if the minister could give favourable consideration to that request, e (4:10 p.m.)
I have taken more time than I intended, but I feel very strongly about these three items and I could not afford to miss the opportunity of placing them before the house and the minister for consideration.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I only wish to take a few moments to raise a couple of points. Although I have been a member of the veterans committee, I have not been able to participate in their meetings in the last few months. Nevertheless I would like to place these suggestions before the committee of the whole. First of all, I wish to speak on veterans allowances. It might be that my contribution will prove to be somewhat irrelevant, except for the fact that it concerns veterans and the allowances to which they are entitled.
Before I begin, may I extend my sincere appreciation of the services rendered by the departmental authorities present with us this afternoon. This matter which we are considering is usually beyond the area of those things which we as politicians consider to be important, but I believe that these officials are doing a good job in the area of the policy before them.
I will not speak in particular about the veterans who are eligible for a larger veterans allowance but I wish to speak of veterans who are in receipt of a small service pension and are unable to earn a livelihood, but cannot obtain other assistance because of the
June 15, 1966

veterans allowance they are receiving. I feel the minister should use his good offices to influence the government to ensure that such a pension income will not prevent war veterans from receiving additional benefits under the War Veterans Allowance Act. I know of several cases in the province of Ontario where welfare payments are made according to the elegibility clauses currently effective in the provincial welfare plan. As I said, this may not be immediately relevant to the war veterans allowances, but it is relevant in regard to veterans who find themselves in the position I have described.
My next comment, Mr. Chairman, regards the matter of the Hong Kong veterans. I fully agree with the policy which has been adopted in this regard, that is that such benefits would be extended to all ex-prisoners of war.
I may point out that both the minister and I have knowledge of this matter because we both found ourselves in exactly similar circumstances. I do not wish for one moment to detract from the need of the Hong Kong veterans; nevertheless I wish to point out that I have information on cases that are equally important and demand equal consideration to that which was given the Hong Kong group. Only last Saturday I received a telegram from the wife of a front gunner with whom I had the privilege of serving, and who died of arteriosclerosis very quickly and unexpectedly.
A series of such occurrences has taken place in the last ten years. I also know of another case of a very close friend of mine from Port Credit who has suffered from the illness, and I could name some other cases in the minister's province of which he knows. I should like to point out that one does not usually find such an advanced stage of arteriosclerosis in people of this age, so these are unusual cases. I therefore wish to ask the minister to give every consideration to this group as well, as I am sure he will.

I was also a member of the veterans committee which has approved these estimates in principle and in detail. As a member of that committee I wish to join the previous speakers in extending thanks for the industry and fairness of our committee chairman, the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry.
However, I rise today with the express purpose of paying tribute to the Minister of Veterans Affairs and also to comment on a situation which was uncovered during our
Supply-Veterans Affairs investigation of the operations of his department. Some time ago I personally congratulated the Minister of Veterans Affairs, Hon. Roger Teillet, because about two years ago hospitals within the purview of the Department of Veterans Affairs introduced a shift differential rate of pay in their operation procedure. This advanced method of treating employees was one that could have been a mountain peak in labour negotiations, conciliation and arbitration for the dominion. However, in our examination of the operations of the medical services of the department an amazing situation disclosing interference by the Civil Service Commission was uncovered, and I wish to draw it to the attention of the house.
Although we are now considering item 1 in the estimates I wish to refer to an item under vote 30 which deals with overtime for the fiscal year 1966-67 which is estimated at $800,000 while in the year 1965-66 it amounted to $630,000. The sum of $800,000 to the uninitiated seems to be a tremendous amount of money to be paying for overtime, but I am advised that it also covers shift differentials. However, it seems to me that the situation which was uncovered in our investigation of the various details of the operation of this department is amazing, and I would go so far as to say it is alarming.
The department is paying a shift differential to the nurses working in the evening and night shifts. We were told that the evening shift starts at 4 p.m. and runs until midnight, while the night shift starts at midnight and runs until 8 a.m., and that the shift differential amounts to 8 cents an hour on the evening shift and 12 cents an hour on the night shift. But what really shocked us was to be told that the Canadian government only pays these nurses a shift differential of 8 cents an hour on the evening shift between 6 p.m. and midnight and 12 cents an hour on the night shift between midnight and 6 a.m. This means that we do not pay these nurses a shift differential from 4 to 6 p.m. nor do we pay them a shift differential from 6 to 8 a.m.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
If I may be allowed to refer to another department of government when we are discussing the estimates on the Department of Veterans Affairs, I should like to point out that I am also a member of the committee on health and welfare. Under that department we find a number of hospitals for Indians and
June 15, 1966

Supply-Veterans Affairs Eskimos. When I made inquiries as to whether or not shift differentials were being paid in the hospitals falling under the Department of National Health and Welfare, I was surprised to find that some of the highly placed officers of the department were not too certain whether shift differentials were being paid. We reminded them of the shift differentials that were being paid by the Department of Veterans Affairs, and they advised they would make a report the following day.
It was only yesterday that we received a typewritten report from the Department of National Health and Welfare with regard to shift differentials in these hospitals. I must read part of it to you because it also covers shift differentials in the Department of Veterans Affairs. This statement is entitled, "Clarification of procedures relating to the payment of overtime and shift differentials in the Department of National Health and Welfare". I quote:
During the committee's review of vote 20, questions were raised concerning the payment of overtime and shift differentials to employees in medical services. These procedures are governed by the civil service regulations-
We are told, however, that in the matter of overtime, operating classes under exempt staff regulations may be granted leave or compensated in cash at the rate of time and one half. In so far as shift differentials are concerned the report states:
A shift differential is paid to employees who work regular shifts between the hours of 6 p.m. and 6 a.m. The shift differential for the evening shift, i.e., between 6 p.m. and midnight is 8 cents per hour and between the hours of midnight and 6 a.m. is 12 cents per hour.
Now, I asked the highly placed authority in the Department of National Health and Welfare if he knew of another employer anywhere in Canada who did not pay the full shift differential for each hour in the shift, that is the evening shift or the night shift. The gentleman, and the several assistants he had with him, nodded their heads in great surprise and said no, they did not know of a single other employer who refused to pay the shift differential for each hour of the shift, as was being done by the government of Canada. When I asked them only yesterday who would be responsible for such a ridiculous situation as a shift differential being paid only for certain hours of a shift, I was told that this aspect would come under the Treasury Board, by authority of the Financial Administration Act.

I intend to follow the matter further because I think it is ridiculous for the government of Canada to be paying these wages under a shift differential heading, when people expect the government to be a model employer and to treat the employees in the civil service with decency, and with regard for the prevailing wage practices throughout the nation as a whole.
When I congratulated the Minister of Veterans Affairs two years ago-and I congratulated him with a sincere and full heart-for having established shift differentials in the payment of nurses in the 11 hospitals, I felt confident that the establishment of shift differentials for nurses in these 11 hospitals right across the Dominion of Canada would serve as a model to other active treatment and chronic hospitals. I felt it might even serve as a spur to other hospitals to establish shift differentials for their employees. I have been rather distressed by the lack of response on the part of other hospitals to shift differentials. I trust that when the minister is summing up matters just before we pass these estimates, and I sincerely hope they will be passed this afternoon, he will make some comment with regard to Sunnybrook Hospital in Toronto.
Sunnybrook Hospital in Toronto is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Veterans Affairs. We understand that if final arrangements are completed it will be turned over to the University of Toronto as a teaching hospital on July 1. The minister has been kind enough to make a statement to me just now, and he says it will not be July 1. I draw to the attention of the minister, for whom I have the highest regard, that there are reports circulating in Toronto and central Ontario to the effect that one of the stumbling blocks to the transfer of Sunnybrook Hospital to the University of Toronto as a teaching hospital is the opposition in the province of Ontario to shift differentials which prevail in Sunnybrook Hospital at the moment. This hospital of course will immediately come under the wing of the Ontario Hospital Services Commission. It certainly begins to look as if there is active opposition in Ontario at the provincial level toward shift differentials in hospitals. It is felt that if Sunnybrook Hospital is transferred, with the ridiculous shift differentials that are now being paid, it might serve as a precedent to establish shift differentials elsewhere throughout Ontario in active treatment hospitals.
June 15, 1966	COMMONS
I have referred to this situation because in Toronto we have Riverdale Chronic Hospital in the riding of Broadview, the employees of which were governed by a municipal employees contract. Employment conditions at Riverdale Hospital were certainly much better than in any other hospital in the Toronto area. In fact, at Riverdale Hospital, when the last collective agreement was signed in June, 1964, the starting rate for registered nurses in other hospitals in Toronto was $335 per month and the starting rate at Riverdale was also $335. This increased to $355 after three months of service. In addition to this $20 per month differential there were other certain conditions which were not available in other hospitals such as shift premiums, premium pay for holidays worked, uniform allowance, time and a half for overtime, etc. These conditions made Riverdale sufficiently attractive that it had a full complement of staff for the equipment available in the hospital at that time.
What has happened is that the municipal government in Toronto has now detached Riverdale Hospital from the municipal services and it has been established under an independent board of trustees or governors. It has been placed indirectly under the Ontario Hospital Services Commission, and every step is being taken to eliminate these fringe benefits which the Riverdale Hospital nurses enjoyed, as well as the hospital staff, while they were members of the municipal union. It looks to me as though there is a concerted effort afoot in the province of Ontario to knock hospital wages down to the lowest level from the Ottawa River to Kenora.
Now, in this connection I sincerely hope that the Sunnybrook Hospital, when turned over to the University of Toronto, will continue to pay a shift differential, ridiculously low as it is. I hope the minister will ask assurance it will be maintained as a beacon light in this regard. In January of this year a decision of an arbitration board adjudicating on a dispute between Welland County General Hospital and its service employees was handed down. The mmebers of this arbitration board were Professor H. W. Arthurs, J. David Cromarty and Drummond Wren. In the course of their decision, these gentlemen had some comments that are interesting. They pointed out that in Ontario the employees of hospitals cannot strike, but have to submit to 23033-409

Supply-Veterans Affairs arbitration. Professor Arthurs writes, as recorded on page 6 of the report:
But arbitration is made to substitute for the srtike and should therefore likewise be considered an exercise in discovering labour market realities. This being so, it is to relevant wage comparisons that we must look...
We would also consider the following factors to be relevant:
1. Difficulties encountered by the hospital in recruiting and holding staff (some evidence of the hospital's failure to pay a level of wages high enough to attract workers on the local labour market.)
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Further on page 10 Professor Arthurs writes:
This adjustment is important in our calculations because the general labour market obviously affects hospital wages by drawing away hospital workers if substantial disparities in pay levels develop.
There is no question that the wages paid in other industries are affecting the employment of the staffs of hospitals, and these wages should be on a parity. One of the great benefits in the labour market of unionized contracts is shift differentials.
I should like to refer to the question of premium pay for holidays. Why should nurses who are employed in war veterans hospitals be expected to work on Christmas day, Good Friday, civic holidays, Labour day, Victoria day, Canada day and the other national holidays for the same wages as they would receive on an ordinary Monday or Friday in a regular work week? I suggest to the Minister of Veterans Affairs that he should authorize premium pay for the statutory holidays which have been enumerated by this parliament.
I would draw his attention to the fact that in 1964, in manufacturing as a whole, almost three quarters of a million workers, representing 82 per cent of the total, received premium pay for holidays. Mr. Chairman, I am in the very fortunate position at this point in the consideration of the estimates of having had nearly everything said already for me. However, there are one or two points I should like briefly to cover.
As we know, the estimates have been discussed in the committee on veterans affairs. They have been as thoroughly discussed this year as they were in past years. I should like to add my words of commendation along with those of other hon. members to the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry, and also to the vice chairman of the committee. These two gentlemen were a pleasure to work with, and I am sure that I am echoing the sentiments of other members of the committee when I say that.
The standing committee on veterans affairs is a non-partisan committee, which is the way it should be. There was no partisanship in wartime in this respect. Veterans legislation has been based, and for the most part amended over the years, on non-partisan principles, and it is only right that in the committee there should also be this spirit of non-partisanship.

The right hon. gentleman who is my leader mentioned a few moments ago the number of committees of the House of Commons and the difficulty of getting quorums for them. The hon. member for Kootenay West very rightly said that in this committee there is an especially high record of attendance, and this is all to the good.
I think that one of the faults of our committee system in this house is the fact that we bunch all our committee work into the latter stages of the session. Members who are perhaps deeply interested in four or five subjects find that the whip is after them, trying to get them to attend two or three committees at once which, of course, is just impossible.
I think experience has taught us that it is
much wiser for members to serve on only two, or perhaps three, committees at the most, in which event they can attend the committees. Many of those who serve on the veterans affairs committee devote the major part of their attention to it and perhaps one other committee. That is the case as far as I am concerned. Therefore I would suggest to the government at this time that if the work of these committees could start a little earlier in the session, we could devote more time to committees. It did not take the veterans affairs committee very long, once the committee started to consider the estimates, to clear them up.
Another matter which has been touched on is the report on the Hong Kong veterans. I have read many reports made by commissioners and others, but I do not think I have ever seen or read a finer report than that which has been prepared by Dr. Richardson. This gentleman brought sympathy and understanding, and of course all of his medical and administrative knowledge, to bear on this particular subject, and he has presented an exceptionally fine report.
Many members have been deeply interested in this particular problem of the Hong Kong veterans over the years. My colleague from Athabasca has been pressing this matter for many years, as have many others. I have been interested in the subject for a very special reason. The Royal Rifles of Canada, one of the two battalions which served in Hong Kong, were recruited almost exclusively from the eastern townships, the Gaspe area and Restigouche county in northern New Brunswick. This is my part of Canada, Mr. Chairman, and so many of my friends were

in Hong Kong. I saw them before they went there, and I had the opportunity to see them as soon as they arrived home; and there is no question about the maltreatment which these men received while in Hong Kong.
As I said, Dr. Richardson undertook this particular task, to which sympathetic consideration was given by the committee, and he has written a very fine report. Here again I must commend my friend, the chairman of the committee, for the very fine job he did in this regard. I know how hard he has worked; and he has another month's hard work ahead of him before the middle of July.
I omitted at the beginning of my remarks to commend the members of the Department of Veterans Affairs, the chairman of the Pension Commission, the chairman of the War Veterans Allowance Board and all the other officials for the exceptionally fine work they have done. The Department of Veterans Affairs is very fortunate in the calibre of men and women who have served it over the years.
In my own case, my relationship has been an especially happy one. This does not mean of course that all of the cases which I have taken to the Pension Commission, for example, or to the War Veterans Allowance Board, under Colonel Cromb, have been adjudicated upon in the way 1 had hoped; but I do know that they have given careful and thorough consideration to these cases, and if they could not be ruled upon as I had hoped, then it was not their fault. They must follow the regulations and the act, of course.
Very brief mention, Mr. Chairman, has been made of the commission headed by Mr. Justice Mervyn Wood, who is looking into the organization of the Pension Commission. Again we have here an excellent man. I have known Mr. Justice Wood for many years. We served together on the dominion command of the Canadian Legion many years ago, and I look forward to his report. If I am not mistaken, I understand that this report will also be referred to the standing committee for study, which I gather is a not too common a procedure. Nevertheless if this be the case the report will receive careful consideration.

When my leader was speaking a few moments ago he raised the question of veterans pensions. I believe something must now be done to increase the pensions paid to veterans. What veterans are paid may seem a

Supply-Veterans Affairs considerable sum to certain people; but everything is relative. If in the 'thirties they had been getting what a veteran is receiving now, they would have been able to live, if not like millionaires, then almost like them. But we are living in a different age and today we are facing the tremendous problems caused by inflation.
Too many of us in government and elsewhere, are prone to hide our heads in the sand rather than admit the tremendous increase which has taken place in the cost of living. In the United States and in this country I believe we are now on the verge of runaway inflation. The people upon whom the burden falls most heavily are the recipients of war veterans allowances, those receiving pensions under the Pension Act, civil service superannuates, and others on fixed incomes which they can do nothing to increase.
All of us know what organized labour can do; we have had an example of that in the last few days. They can strike, and in many cases they can get substantial increases. Pensioners and those on war veterans allowances have nobody to speak for them but ourselves. We must speak for them, and I urge the minister to consider this question very deeply, now, and to recommend a substantial increase. I realize he will have to face Treasury Board, but I ask him to bring his full talents and energy to this particular matter.
The hon. member for Kootenay West mentioned the Legion convention. This convention was held, as we know, in Montreal in May and some of us had the opportunity of attending. The Legion has had excellent leadership over the years. It is a fine organization dedicated to the welfare of all veterans. In the man who was elected this year to head the legion for the next two years, Mr. Ronald MacBeath, of Moncton, the Legion will have an exceptional leader. Mr. MacBeath has been a personal friend of mine for a long time. I know of his many fine qualities and I think the government as well as the Legion will benefit from his wise counsel.
I will not spend any further time discussing the estimates themselves. They have been examined very carefully by a good committee. I simply commend them to hon. members of this house so that they may now be passed.

Supply-Veterans Affairs on the estimates to the Department of Veterans Affairs to point out to the minister the discrimination which still prevails against French Canadians in his department and the agencies which come under his jurisdiction.
I understand that the minister is not entirely responsible for such a situation, because he inherited it from his predecessors and the previous governments. But since we will be commemorating the centennial next year, an occasion when life in Canada must be celebrated throughout the country, I think it would be appropriate to remedy as many cases of injustice as possible. To that effect, I ask the minister to make an unofficial inquiry within his department and its various agencies; he will easily find out, if he does not know it already after the numerous complaints made, that French Canadians in his department and other agencies under his jurisdiction, as well as the French Canadians who deal with his department's agencies, do not get justice and are not treated as they should be in this country.
For instance, Mr. Chairman, I refer the minister to page 17 of a booklet entitled; "The last chance" which I wrote in 1963. He can get a copy of it right here in the library. He will find on page 17 that, among the civil servants getting an annual salary of $5,000 or over, there are only 10 per cent of French Canadians. It is the general average in all departments.
If you study the various departments one by one, you will find that the ratio in the Department of Veterans Affairs is lower than that average, that is 9.1 per cent.
Some might bring up the argument, which is sometimes heard, that there are not enough French Canadians in some regions of the country, that the standards of competence are to blame, etc. We are used to such arguments. But I want to point out to the minister a very obvious example which I take in the province of Quebec, more precisely from the Queen Mary hospital in Montreal which comes under his department.
That hospital is located in the province of Quebec, whose population is made up of over 80 per cent of French Canadians. Well, I say that there again we are not getting our fair share and that the minister would be well advised, in the interest of peaceful relations throughout this country and give the necessary directives to the officials of the Queen Mary hospital in Montreal.

He can refer to the answer given by his officials and himself to question No. 1,260 I had put on the order paper a few weeks ago.
I asked a first question. It was after many complaints made to me by constituents in Sherbrooke and the province of Quebec to the effect that when French Canadian veterans went to Montreal to be treated, they could not speak in their own language with the physicians there. They wanted to speak, to explain their symptoms to physicians speaking their language, but they could not, and that in the province of Quebec, stronghold of the French Canadian nation. Well, this is not admissible in 1966.
Mr. Chairman, the first part of my question read as follows:
How many French speaking physicians are there at the Queen Mary hospital in Montreal to admit and examine French speaking veterans.
The answer given me was as follows;
Patients at Queen Mary veterans' hospital are examined and admitted from the out patient clinic. This is staffed by 10 part-time general practitioners. Three of these are French speaking.
Well, Mr. Chairman, in the province of Quebec where the great majority of the people are French Canadians, out of these ten physicians, only three are French Canadians. I surely do not want to be told that with all the excellence of its medical body and its physicians, the province of Quebec does not have enough qualified physicians to be able to treat our veterans at the Queen Mary hospital. We should have a majority of French speaking physicians in that hospital coming under the jurisdiction of the department.
Another part of the question was as follows:
What Is the total number of medical practitioners or specialists at this hospital, and of this number, how many are French speaking?
The answer was:
There are a total of 148 part-time medical practitioners and specialists at the hospital. Of these, 40 are French.
There again, Mr. Chairman, less than a third. Well, this is unfair, the complaints are well-founded, and supported by official statistics given to us here in the house. We do not complain on a sentimental basis; we complain on matter of representation which should be given to us.
As far as the other parts of the question are concerned, the minister could find answers showing this adverse and discriminatory situation.

In part 5 of my question, for instance, I asked:
What Is the total number of... and other staff employed at this hospital, and of this number, how many are French speaking?
Again, the situation is disastrous. In the case of nurses, for instance, out of a total of 179 only 83 are French speaking, that is less than half.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to dwell on the matter any longer, but I feel that it is my duty to remind the hon. minister of the situation. I know the minister is favourably disposed, that he endeavours to do a good job, but we would appreciate it greatly if he immediately made an informal investigation, in his department and its agencies, and more particularly at the Queen Mary hospital. Even if, as we are told, there are three doctors out of ten, or 40 doctors out of 148, most of the French Canadian veterans from Sherbrooke and the area come back with grievances, and complain that when they go to Queen Mary hospital they cannot converse in French.
They always have to deal with an English speaking doctor, one who does not understand French. Quite frequently, the veteran comes back-and this affects his health-and his allowance is revised, or decreased or refused precisely because he was unable to speak freely and frankly with a doctor speaking his own tongue, in the province of Quebec.
So these are real grievances. Questions arise in one's mind when discussing the first report of the Laurendeau-Dunton Commission, which report establishes that there is a serious crisis in Canada, a crisis which has its root in Quebec, in spite of what newspapers say in different provinces. Attempts have been made to hush the problem, but it exists, Mr. Chairman. The crisis is serious, but it is not insoluble. That is why French Canadians, in 1966, are asking for a solution from the ministers, from the government, who, in certain spheres, have indicated favourable dispositions, especially the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) through his new policy on bilingualism. Even if it does not extend very far, steps are being taken in the right direction. If we want to solve those problems, French Canadians must at long last be treated as they deserve, so that the centennial to be celebrated next year might truly be of special significance to them.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to take part in this debate. I join all those who agree to the veterans' requests. They ask for many things, but it really comes down to very little. They ask for a better treatment and for a higher pension so as to be able to live decently. They ask that their pension be raised in accordance with the present cost of living.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to tell the minister that I am full of admiration for his good work, his spirit of self-denial and for everything he does for the veterans. The minister is a worthy man. I saw him at work in many places and, in my opinion, he does honour to Canadians and to the department for which he is responsible.
Now, I agree with the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), who spoke a while

June 15, 1966
Supply-Veterans Affairs ago, when he says that French Canadians are not sufficiently represented in the hospitals in key positions. I agree with him in that respect. I know that the minister, a man of good will, is going to do something in this regard.
Now, I will come to the veterans. I am from the county of Compton and I was told that Compton contributed more Canadians who took part in the Japanese war than any other riding. It is an honour for me to represent this constituency and I want to honour them. Now, my fellow-citizens have been ill-treated, as we say; they were submitted to an awful treatment. Because of the atrocities they suffered they are entitled to our admiration, our consideration, our spirit of co-operation and fairness. I think they were the victims of injustice in some cases. Indeed, these veterans were not treated with all the dignity and justice they were entitled to. Consequently, I would be remiss in not defending them in that respect.
Mr. Chairman, we were able during these awful wars to provide them with everything they needed. We have provided them with means of transport and with a pension for themselves and for their family; we have treated them very well during the war. We have even promised them that the old days were over in Canada, the dark days, the days of hardship. We have asked them to fight for civilization, for our basic freedoms, for religion, for security, for what is dearest to our hearts. They have agreed to defend all these things. For us Canadians, for the protection of our laws and freedoms, those people did all we had asked them to do.
Mr. Chairman, since we have provided them with all those things during the war, since we have promised them a lot, I believe that now that the war is over we should find it easy to keep our promises.
During the war, Mr. Chairman, men were not working, they were destroying. Many soldiers were busy destroying. They were neither producers nor builders.
They were not engaged in production but in destruction. Canadians who then remained in Canada contributed to this huge destruction.
Now the war is over. The men have returned home and many of them contribute to Canadian production, thus increasing the volume of our products, and are they to believe that there is a shortage of goods in Canada, that Canada cannot afford to provide for their welfare needs?

Well, Mr. Chairman, it does not make sense. Canada has everything to feed and clothe those people adequately. It did it in wartime and it can do it in peacetime.
A large number of people need security, need us, need justice in this country. Some are sick, though this is denied in certain quarters.

So, I am in agreement with the Leader of the Opposition and with the members of all parties in this house who are siding with the veterans.

Mr. Chairman, I rise simply to endorse a suggestion made to the committee earlier this afternoon by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, namely that the minister, his department and the government consider the extension of war veterans' allowance benefits to those under the age of 60.1 have in mind several cases from my own riding, one of which I shall relate and which I think backs up the contention of the hon. member.
This case concerns a younger man who served in world war II after entering the army in excellent physical condition, but emerged in a poor physical category. For one reason or another he was not given the benefit of a pension. His condition was an ulcerous one, obviously a nervous condition, and since he applied himself fully to his military duties it is difficult to see how this condition could have arisen from any cause other than military service. But the fact is that he was not given the benefit of a pension and therefore finds himself, after good war service, in the position where he is not able to work at a level he probably would have attained had he not undertaken to serve his country. In short, Mr. Chairman, the income of this man is of a low level, and he has serious responsibilities.
There are other cases like this in my riding but I shall not deal with them in detail. I mention this one as a specific instance and I heartily endorse the suggestion of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. I realize that there are difficulties in the way of bringing in a formula which would work. There would be people who would try to take advantage of such a formula. But the fact is that our veterans legislation is supposed to err, if it errs at all, on the side of generosity and giving all doubt to the veteran. This reinforces me in my suggestion that the request of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo be given great consideration by the department and I ask the minister to do this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In response to the invitation from the hon. member for Ontario I want to say that the Minister of Finance is having a hard time, which is usual for all ministers of finance, although I do not think his difficulties are any greater than those of his predecessors.
We are at a time, in our nation's history in which there are financial problems, but I am very glad to say that they are associated with great prosperity. I think we all like to live at a time when the demand for goods and for the services of our working people is not deficient. But if we want to ensure that our prosperity will continue for a good time into the future, policies of restraint are necessary, restraint which applies-as I said in speaking on the Bank of Canada Act the other day-in the field of monetary policy as well as in other fields.
I am therefore very happy to present my estimates for the consideration of the house, and I wait with bated breath for the comments from the opposition.

I think the minister has made a most inadequate statement in commencing these estimates. He has dealt almost not at all with the important issues 23033-4101
Supply-Finance
which face the economy of this country. I confess I am somewhat surprised that in view of the controversy that has existed between the minister and the hon. member for Davenport he has not sought to bring before the house his own point of view and to express clearly what the policy of the government may be, as opposed to the policy of the grey eminence of the Liberal party.
The fact that the minister has refrained from making any major statement is, I think, an indication that he is permitting the policies of the Department of Finance to drift. Apparently what he has established as the basic economic and fiscal policy of the government is one of drifting. We saw this in the budget which was a stand pat budget. The fact is that since that time there has been nothing at all to indicate that the hon. gentleman has any imagination or any vivid approach to the serious problems that confront the country today.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Now, sir, I had not expected the estimates of the Department of Finance would be called this afternoon. I had intended to make a rather extensive presentation on one particular subject. Twice before at this session of parliament I have mentioned in some detail the question of increases in pensions for retired civil servants. I think the proper time to deal with this subject, and to have it out with the Minister of Finance, is now on item 1. The minister and the Prime Minister, in their negotiations and discussions with various civil service organizations, have been adamant. I say to the minister today that it is not good enough for him or the Prime Minister to take the attitude which they have taken.
There has been only one occasion when there has been any increase in the pensions of retired civil servants, and that was in the year 1958. Initially, it was an estimate and was crystallized in legislation in the pension adjustment act of 1959. I say to the minister that there are many retired civil servants across this country who are suffering grave hardship by reason of his adamant refusal to make the increases which I believe are entirely justified. This is not an area in which policy has not been established already by this parliament. Parliament has set its seal of approval on the policy of increases when they are needed to meet the cost of living. It did so in 1958 and 1959.
It is not as if we alone had done this. This procedure has been adopted, as the minister

June 15, 1966
Supply-Finance
well knows, in the United States and the United Kingdom. I think it was on Monday last that I read into the record some of the statements which have been made in the United Kingdom as contained in that Hansard for November, 1965. There were at least six pension adjustment increases for retired civil servants in that country. I then put on the record as well what the position is in the United States. These two countries have set a model and an example with regard to pension adjustments, just as this country set a model and an example in the enactment of the pension adjustment act.
I suggest that this is the example the minister ought to follow, and he ought to follow it at this session of parliament. If the minister had received all the representations which I have received from time to time from retired civil servants across this country, he would know the genuine hardships and injustices that there are by reason of the decline in the value of the dollar. Some of these persons have been retired for many years, and when they made their contributions they were in dollars of an entirely different value than the dollars they are taking out of the fund today. In some cases these dollars have a value as low as 50 per cent of the value of the dollars they put into the superannuation account. I do not believe that this country should treat its retired public servants in such a shoddy, shabby way as the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have insisted upon doing. I believe if he tested the will of the members of this house he would find they were all in favour of increases, and of an updating of the pension adjustment act to bring genuine justice to these retired civil servants.
I know there is a disposition to get ahead with these estimates. I want to say to the minister, however, that I should like a full answer in respect of this matter. I want the minister to try to vindicate in some way the adamant stand that has been taken. I cannot understand how there could he any vindication of it. However, I hope he will at least try to rationalize the point of view he has taken. I do appeal to him, if he will, to listen to reason, to listen to what I believe is a popular demand to introduce legislation in this respect at this session of parliament.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I was rising only part way in the hope that the Minister of Finance was going to get up and give the answer that ought to be given to the plea that has just

been made once again by the hon. member for Carleton. I agree with the hon. member that at some point we have got to have this matter out. I think it is disgraceful, the way in which these people have been pushed around, encouraged and then discouraged, put off and told to wait for this piece of legislation or that; and finally we seem to have reached a point where we cannot get anywhere at all.
I had hoped that with the amount of attention being paid in this session to civil service matters and civil service pensions, particularly in relation to Bill No. C-193, we would get action. However, the Minister of National Revenue, who is piloting that bill through the house on behalf of the Minister of Finance, has taken the very adamant position that that bill deals only with people now in the civil service, and not with retired persons. We seem therefore to be thrown back upon the tender mercies of the Minister of Finance.
Tender?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I hope that question is on the record because it will indicate that I am not the only one who wonders just how tender those mercies are. Our purpose in this debate is to try to find out. Frankly, I hope the minister will try to give us his reasoning with respect to this matter. I do not see how the government can stand against this principle. The hon. member for Carleton has referred to the action taken by the Diefenbaker government when it brought in the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act. I suggest that act did establish as a principle the willingness of parliament to deal with this matter. If the present government is sensitive about having Conservative practice thrown at it from time to time, I remind this government that it is the one that accepted the principle of escalation in pensions. This has been done in respect of two pieces of legislation. There is, both in the Canada Pension Plan and in the Old Age Security Act, a provision for escalating pensions. In one case, the escalation can take place both prior to the time one receives a pension and afterwards. In the other case, it applies only after the pensions have been paid.
I believe this was a very good move that the government made in allowing the principle of escalation in at least two of our pension acts. I am sure the reason the government did that, the reason the government
June 15, 1966

was prepared to ask parliament to do it, was that it had come to the realization that after people retire they still have certain rights as members of the community. Those rights include the right to be able to live on the pensions that are awarded to them on the basis of their service. The right to live in the years after one retires, Mr. Chairman, includes the right to be able to keep up with the cost of living, and also the right to be able to keep up with the rising standard of living. I know that most people who write letters to us appealing for pension increases base their arguments on the increased cost of living, and that is a sufficient argument to make it necessary that something be done.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I think an equally valid argument is the rising standard of living. When conditions of life improve all round, those improved conditions exert pressures on people which are just as real as pressures which arise from an increased cost of living. Because a person retired before there was television, there is no reason that that person should not enjoy television in his retirement. Because a person retired before certain other improvements took place in our standard of living, that is no reason that he should not enjoy these other improvements. We would not say that some members of a family shall enjoy such affluence as the family has, but that other members shall not.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, because of these two reasons-the rising cost of living and the rising standard of living-I believe that parliament has gladly accepted the principle contained in the amendments to the Old Age Security Act and in the Canada Pension Plan, that there shall be escalation of pensions, yes even after they have been put in pay. If the government has been prepared to do this in general legislation, I submit that the government should do it for its own retired employees.
I insist there is no ground at all, in principle, for opposing that for which we are asking on behalf of our retired civil servants. The argument is sometimes made that they were employed on a contractual basis, and that these people have to accept the terms of that contract. But every year or so we amend the terms of the contract in our various pension acts. We are doing it this session in Bill No. C-193. We are not only doing the job of integration and all the rest of it, but we are taking care of the various anomalies. Every time we do this we admit that as the
Supply-Finance
statute stood before it was not perfect. Why should these people who are retired be forced to be the victims of the imperfections of the legislation, or the formula, or the contract made in years gone by?
The hon, member for Carleton referred to the fact that action in this area has been taken in the United States and in the United Kingdom. It has also been taken in a number of the provinces in this country. I have not the list in front of me, but a number of them have done so. In the province of Ontario I know that arrangements have been made to improve the pensions of teachers after they have retired. In my own city of Winnipeg the municipal administration has provided that pensions of retired civic employees can be increased and that provision is there for those who may retire in the future.
The idea that we have this responsibility to our retired workers when they leave our employ is so widely accepted that I cannot understand why this realization has not impressed itself on the hearts and the mercies of those who sit on the treasury benches. One of the matters which is terribly disheartening to these people has been the way in which their hopes have been buoyed up, only to be put down again.
Even after this government came into power there were times when this matter was being considered. The former minister of finance, the hon. member for Davenport, assured us on a number of occasions that this question would be considered. Representatives of these people came to Ottawa and had interviews with cabinet ministers, I believe an interview even with the Prime Minister, and they were led to believe at one time that when the Canada Pension Plan was passed their problem would be dealt with. They were also led to believe that when the subject of old age pensions was dealt with their problem would be considered. But the recent letters they have received, mainly from the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, have given them the impression that this government has closed the door. I do not think that the government is reflecting either the will of parliament or the will of the people of the country in the position it is taking.
As the hon. member for Carleton says, it is apparently this minister with whom we must have it out. I almost said that it is this minister whom we must "have it out with", but I thought I had better be precise in dealing with the Minister of Finance. The

June 15, 1966
Supply-Finance
Prime Minister passes the problem to him. The Minister of National Revenue says that it does not come under his legislation. If it is a financial question, then it is this minister who must make the decision, and I think we should hear from him. I hope that what he has to say will be satisfactory; if not we will have to keep at him.

Mr. Chairman, ever since I have been the member for Ottawa East I have never let the opportunity pass to make this plea to the Minister of Finance. Almost yearly for the past 20 years I have asked him to do something to escalate the pensions of retired civil servants. Those of us who live in Ottawa know the need for this escalation. When our civil servants contributed to the superannuation fund they expected they would be able to retire with sufficient to afford them a certain standard of living. Instead of that, Mr. Chairman, during the past 10 to 15 years many of them have been living like people who, certainly, one would think from their present standard of living had been engaged in some other kind of occupation.
I would urge on the Minister of Finance at this time, when we come to consider amendments to the superannuation acts, when the Canada Assistance Plan is introduced, and when we discuss legislation for the benefit of those who are in similar situations, to see to it that we look after our own employees even in a better way than those of private industry, other governments, provincial or municipal, or governments of other countries. I hope that the day will soon come when this parliament will be proud to say that our retired civil servants now have the treatment to which they are entitled.
